summary: Counting with only the digits 0 and 1, where each place is a power of two.
detail: Binary suits electronics because a switch is either off or on. 1011₂ = 8 + 0 + 2 + 1 = 11.

summary: Base-16 counting using 0–9 and A–F, used because one hex digit maps exactly to four bits.
detail: 0xFF is 255 and 0x2A is 42. Colours on the web are written this way: #RRGGBB.

summary: A single binary digit: 0 or 1, the smallest unit of information.
detail: With n bits you can represent 2^n distinct values: 8 bits give 256, 32 bits give about 4.3 billion.

summary: Eight bits, holding 256 distinct values (0–255 unsigned).
detail: A kilobyte is strictly 1000 bytes (SI), while a kibibyte (KiB) is 1024 bytes — the reason a '1 TB' drive shows less after formatting.

summary: 1024 bytes — the binary multiple, as opposed to the decimal kilobyte of 1000 bytes.
detail: The IEC defined KiB, MiB, GiB and TiB in 1998 to end the confusion; many tools still label MiB as 'MB'.

summary: A finite, ordered set of steps that turns an input into an answer.
detail: An algorithm must terminate and be unambiguous. Different algorithms for the same job differ enormously in speed — sorting a million items with bubble sort is far slower than with quicksort.

summary: A way to describe how an algorithm's cost grows with input size, ignoring constants.
detail: O(n) grows in step with the input, O(n²) with its square, and O(log n) barely grows at all — a binary search halves the problem each step.

summary: How computers store fractional numbers: a sign, a binary fraction and an exponent, per IEEE 754.
detail: Values are stored in binary, so most decimals cannot be exact — 0.1 + 0.2 prints as 0.30000000000000004. OmniCalc therefore formats to a sane precision and shows exact fractions when it can.

summary: A value that is either true or false, named after George Boole.
detail: Booleans combine with AND, OR and NOT, and they are the basis of the logic gates inside every processor.

summary: A physical circuit implementing a boolean operation, from which every processor is built.
detail: NAND alone is functionally complete: any other gate can be built from repeated NANDs, which is why chip designers use it as the primitive.

summary: A function that maps data of any size to a fixed-size fingerprint.
detail: Used for hash tables, file integrity and password storage. A good hash is fast, spreads values evenly, and changes completely for a one-bit input change.

summary: A routine that calls itself on a smaller version of the problem, with a base case that stops it.
detail: Factorial is the classic example: n! = n × (n−1)! with 0! = 1. Every recursive solution can be rewritten iteratively — often at the cost of clarity.

summary: Transforming data so only holders of the key can read it.
detail: Symmetric ciphers (AES) use one shared key; asymmetric ones (RSA, ECC) use a public/private pair, which is how TLS negotiates secure connections.

summary: An organised store of data that can be queried and updated efficiently.
detail: Relational databases keep tables that join through keys and guarantee ACID transactions; key-value and document stores trade some guarantees for scale.

summary: The documented way one piece of software asks another to do something.
detail: A good API hides internals behind stable names. OmniCalc itself exposes only a browser UI and no network calls at all.
